mainTopic: When a plague or distant threat calls for a fast, and the hidden merit of ordinary people (רבי יוסי's teaching, the neighborhoods spared, and אבא אומנא)
overview: This amud opens with the end of a ברייתא: three deaths in a city of 500 men count as a דבר only if they happen on three days in a row, not all on one day or spread over four days. רב נחמן בר יצחק challenges רב נחמן בר רב חסדא for fasting over three deaths in one day in דרוקרת, since that follows only רבי מאיר's minority logic about a goring ox. This leads to a warm exchange between the two. רב נחמן בר יצחק quotes רבי יוסי: a person honors his place, proven from הר סיני and the אהל מועד. He ends with the parable of a 'מנה son of a פרס'. Next come two stories where a neighborhood was spared a plague or a fire, not because of a great רב, but because of an ordinary person's kindness. Then the גמרא lists cases where sages fasted over threats that seemed small or far away: locusts, a plague among pigs, a plague in בי חוזאי, and a plague in ארץ ישראל. It explains why each one was still a real danger. The amud ends with אבא אומנא, the bloodletter who received a daily greeting from Heaven for his modesty and generosity, and אביי's test of him, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Deaths in one day or over four days are not a plague
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא finishes its definition of דבר: three deaths in one day, or spread over four days, do not count as a plague.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the three people died on one day, or over four days, this is not a plague.
steps.whatsHappening: We are at the end of a ברייתא that defines a דבר. It says that if the three deaths happened all on one day, or were spread across four days, it is not a plague.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule before this line was that three deaths on three days in a row, in a city of 500 men, is a דבר. This line sets the edges of that rule. One day is too bunched together, and four days is too spread out. Only the pattern of three days in a row counts.

keyTerms.meaning: Plague or pestilence, a reason to declare a public fast

steps.confusionAlert: It sounds backwards that three deaths in ONE day is not a plague, since that seems even worse. The rule is about a steady day-after-day pattern. Deaths bunched into one day can be a one-time event, not a spreading plague. The next steps deal with exactly this question.

phrases.english: On one day or over four days —
phrases.notes: Refers to the three deaths in a city of 500 men.

phrases.english: this is not a plague.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּיוֹם אֶחָד אוֹ בְּאַרְבָּעָה יָמִים אֵין זֶה דֶּבֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא's definition of דבר, which began on the previous amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Three deaths on a single day, or across four days, do not count as a דבר.

steps.title: The story of דרוקרת: a fast after three deaths in one day
steps.stepSummary: In the town of דרוקרת, three people died in one day, and רב נחמן בר רב חסדא declared a תענית.
steps.simpleTranslation: דרוקרת was a city that sent out five hundred foot soldiers, and three dead were carried out of it on one day. רב נחמן בר רב חסדא decreed a fast.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real case that seems to go against the rule we just learned. רב נחמן בר רב חסדא declared a fast over three deaths in one day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דרוקרת fits the size in the ברייתא, since it sent out 500 soldiers. But the three deaths all happened on one day, and the ברייתא just said that is not a דבר. This story sets up the challenge in the next step.

phrases.english: Drokart, a city that sends out
five hundred foot soldiers, it was,
phrases.notes: Exactly the size mentioned in the ברייתא.

phrases.aramaic: וְיָצְאוּ מִמֶּנָּה שְׁלֹשָׁה מֵתִים בְּיוֹם אֶחָד.
phrases.english: and three dead were carried out of it on one day.

phrases.aramaic: גְּזַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר רַב חִסְדָּא תַּעֲנִיתָא.
phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda decreed a fast.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּרוֹקֶרֶת עִיר הַמּוֹצִיאָה חֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת רַגְלִי הֲוַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Presents a real case that seems to go against the rule just stated in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב נחמן בר רב חסדא treated three deaths in one day as a reason to declare a fast.

steps.title: The fast follows only רבי מאיר's reasoning about a goring ox
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק points out that the fast follows רבי מאיר's 'all the more so' logic from the laws of a goring ox. That is a minority view.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: Whose opinion are you following? רבי מאיר's. He said: if an ox gored on separate days, the owner is liable. If it gored close together, all the more so!
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק challenges the fast. He says it only works according to רבי מאיר, whose view is not the accepted halacha.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ox becomes a שור מועד after goring three times. חכמים require three separate days. רבי מאיר argues that goring three times close together, in one day, is even more dangerous, so it counts all the more. Declaring a plague over three deaths in one day uses the same logic, so it rests on רבי מאיר, and we do not follow him.

keyTerms.meaning: According to whom? (asks whose view something follows)
Its gorings were spread apart (on separate days)
Its gorings were close together (on one day)
Is it not all the more so? (an 'even more' argument)
Liable (here, to pay full damages as a forewarned ox)

steps.confusionAlert: רבי מאיר's logic sounds convincing, but the challenge depends on the fact that the halacha does NOT follow him. The point is not that his logic is silly. It is that the accepted view, both for the ox and for a plague, requires a pattern over separate days.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the same rule of 'pattern over separate days' runs through two very different areas: damages caused by an ox, and declaring a public fast.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said:
Like whom? Like Rabbi Meir,
who said: if it spread out its gorings, the owner is liable,
phrases.notes: Speaking about an ox becoming a שור מועד.

phrases.english: if it brought its gorings close together, is it not all the more so?!
phrases.notes: The implied point: halacha is not like רבי מאיר, so the fast is questionable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the fast declared in step 2 by tying it to a minority opinion.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן בר רב חסדא's decision to declare a fast over three deaths in one day
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The fast relies on רבי מאיר's 'close together is even worse' reasoning. The Rabbis reject that reasoning for a goring ox, and the ברייתא rejects it for a plague.

steps.title: An invitation to come live in the community
steps.stepSummary: Impressed by the sharp argument, רב נחמן בר רב חסדא invites רב נחמן בר יצחק to come live with them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר רב חסדא said to רב נחמן בר יצחק: Let the master get up and come to us.
steps.whatsHappening: Instead of arguing back, רב נחמן בר רב חסדא is impressed and invites רב נחמן בר יצחק to come live in his town. This sets up the reply in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The halachic argument ends here, and the challenge is accepted without a defense. The conversation moves to a personal exchange. The invitation sets up the teaching about a person and his place.

keyTerms.meaning: Come to us (come live with us)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב נַחְמָן בַּר רַב חִסְדָּא
phrases.english: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda said to him,
to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak:
Let the master arise and come to us.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the challenge in step 3 with admiration rather than a defense.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב נחמן בר רב חסדא invites רב נחמן בר יצחק to join his community.

steps.title: A person honors his place, not the other way around
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק answers with a ברייתא: רבי יוסי teaches that a place does not give a person honor; a person gives honor to his place.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: We learned in a ברייתא that רבי יוסי says: A person's place does not honor him. Rather, a person honors his place.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק answers the invitation by quoting רבי יוסי. A person's greatness comes from who he is, not from where he lives.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is that moving to a more important place is not what brings honor. Wherever a worthy person lives, he brings honor to that place. So רב נחמן בר יצחק sees no reason to move in order to gain honor.

keyTerms.meaning: We have learned (introduces a תנאי source)

phrases.english: He said to him: We have learned,
Rabbi Yosei says:
It is not a person's place that honors him,
rather, a person honors his place.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא מְקוֹמוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם מְכַבְּדוֹ אֶלָּא אָדָם מְכַבֵּד אֶת מְקוֹמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replies to the invitation in step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רב נחמן בר יצחק would come to live in the community
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He quotes רבי יוסי: a place does not make a person great; a person makes his place great.

steps.title: Proof from הר סיני: holy only while the שכינה was there
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי proves his point from הר סיני. Animals could not graze near it while the שכינה rested there, but once the שכינה left, people could go up.
steps.simpleTranslation: For so we find with הר סיני: as long as the שכינה rested on it, the Torah said, 'Even the sheep and cattle may not graze facing that mountain.' Once the שכינה left it, the Torah said, 'When the shofar sounds long, they may go up the mountain.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי brings a proof from הר סיני. Its holiness came from the שכינה resting there, not from the mountain itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: While the שכינה was on the mountain, even animals were kept away from it. Once the שכינה left, people were allowed to climb it. So the honor of the place depended entirely on who was there, which proves that the person, not the place, brings the honor.

keyTerms.meaning: For so we find (introduces a proof)

steps.whatToRemember: The halachic point: a plague (דבר) requires three deaths on three days in a row. Three deaths in one day counts only according to רבי מאיר's minority logic. The story then turns to רבי יוסי's lesson, proven from הר סיני: a person brings honor to his place, not the place to the person.

phrases.english: For so we find with Mount Sinai,
that as long as the Divine Presence rested upon it,
the Torah said:
"Even the flocks and the herds

phrases.aramaic: אַל יִרְעוּ אֶל מוּל הָהָר הַהוּא״,
phrases.english: shall not graze facing that mountain,"
once the Divine Presence departed from it,
the Torah said:
"When the shofar sounds long, they shall go up the mountain."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides the proof for רבי יוסי's statement in step 5.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוסי's principle that a person honors his place, not the reverse
steps.raayaSupportSource: The verses about הר סיני (Exodus 34:3 and 19:13): the mountain was off-limits only while the שכינה rested on it.

steps.title: Second proof: the Tent of Meeting in the desert
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי brings a second proof from the אהל מועד. While it stood, people with צרעת were sent out of the camp. Once its curtains were rolled up, even זבים and מצורעים could enter that spot.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we also find the same thing with the אהל מועד in the desert. As long as it was set up, the תורה said: 'Send out of the camp every person with צרעת.' Once the curtains were rolled up, זבים and מצורעים were allowed to go in there.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי adds a second example to back up his rule that a place does not honor a person. He uses the אהל מועד, just as he used הר סיני before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ground where the אהל מועד stood was only holy while the משכן was standing on it. Once the curtains were packed up, even people who were טמא could walk there. So the holiness came from what was present, not from the spot itself. That is the point of the ברייתא: a person gives a place its importance, and the place does not give it to him.

keyTerms.meaning: The Tent of Meeting, the portable משכן in the desert
Set up, pitched (said of a tent)
A person with צרעת, a spiritual skin affliction
People with a bodily discharge that makes them טמא

steps.whatToRemember: Holiness and honor come from what or who is present, not from the location itself. Both הר סיני and the אהל מועד show this.
steps.whyThisMatters: This finishes the explanation of why רב נחמן בר יצחק sees no reason to move to דרוקרת for honor. A great place will not make him great, and his greatness does not depend on where he lives.

phrases.english: And so we find with the Tent of Meeting that was in the desert,
that as long as it was set up,
the Torah said:
"And they shall send out of the camp every leper"
once the curtains were rolled up,
phrases.notes: That is, when the משכן was packed up for travel.

phrases.english: zavim and lepers were permitted to enter there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second, parallel proof to the הר סיני proof in step 6.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוסי's rule that a place does not honor a person; a person honors his place.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The פסוק 'וישלחו מן המחנה כל צרוע' together with the fact that the area became permitted once the אהל מועד was packed up.

steps.title: Then I will come to you
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר רב חסדא answers: if you will not come here, then I will come to you to learn.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: If that is so, let me get up and come to you, Master.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר רב חסדא accepts that רב נחמן בר יצחק will not move. So he offers to be the one who moves instead. This sets up the reply in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He agrees with the logic: the place is not what matters, the person is. So if רב נחמן בר יצחק is the great one, it makes sense for the learner to go to the teacher. This turns the original invitation around.

keyTerms.meaning: If so, if that is the case
To the Master, a respectful way of saying 'to you'

phrases.english: He said to him: If so,
phrases.notes: רב נחמן בר רב חסדא is the speaker.

phrases.english: let me get up and come to the Master.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the ברייתא by reversing the original invitation.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Since honor comes from the person, I (the student) should move to you.

steps.title: Better the lesser lineage go to the greater
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק refuses with a parable of coins. A 'מנה son of a פרס' should go to a 'מנה son of a מנה', and not the other way around.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: It is better that a מנה whose father was a פרס should come to a מנה whose father was a מנה. A מנה whose father was a מנה should not come to a מנה whose father was a פרס.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק turns down the offer. He says he should be the one to travel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מנה is a full coin of 100 זוז, and a פרס is half of one. Both men are scholars (each is a 'מנה'). But רב נחמן בר רב חסדא is the son of a great scholar, רב חסדא. רב נחמן בר יצחק's father was an ordinary man. So the one with the lesser lineage should go to the one with the greater lineage, out of respect.

keyTerms.meaning: A coin worth 100 זוז; here, a person of full stature
Half a מנה; here, a person of lesser stature
Son of; here it refers to the father's stature

steps.whatToRemember: Both men show humility. Each one insists that he is the one who should go to the other.
steps.confusionAlert: The 'מנה son of a פרס' is רב נחמן בר יצחק, the speaker himself. He is a great scholar from an ordinary family. He is not calling the other man the lesser one.

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: רב נחמן בר יצחק is the speaker.

phrases.english: Better that a maneh son of a peras should come
to a maneh son of a maneh,
and a maneh son of a maneh should not come
to a maneh son of a peras.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the offer in step 8 and explains why.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Lineage decides who should travel. The scholar from an ordinary family should go to the scholar who is the son of a scholar.

steps.title: Plague in סורא spares רב's neighborhood
steps.stepSummary: A plague struck סורא, but it did not reach the neighborhood of רב. People assumed this was because of רב's great merit.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a plague in סורא, but in רב's neighborhood there was no plague. People concluded that this was because of רב's great merit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new story about a plague. This step only sets up what people assumed. The real explanation comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This links back to the theme of plagues and fasting from earlier in the sugya. The natural guess was that the area was protected by the great רב who lived there. The story is set up so that this guess can be corrected.

keyTerms.meaning: They concluded from it, they assumed

phrases.english: In Sura there was a plague,
but in Rav's neighborhood there was no plague.
They assumed from this
that it was because of Rav's merit, which is great.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new story connected to the theme of plagues from the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: People assumed רב's neighborhood was spared in his merit.

steps.title: The dream: it was the man who lent burial tools
steps.stepSummary: A dream revealed that רב's merit was too great to be used on such a small matter. The neighborhood was actually saved by a man who lent out his hoe and shovel for burials.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was shown to them in a dream: רב, whose merit is very great, this is too small a thing for רב. Rather, it was because of a certain man who lends out his hoe and shovel for burials.
steps.whatsHappening: A dream corrects what people assumed. The protection came from a simple man's kindness, not from רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's merit is so great that it would be used for far bigger miracles. Saving one neighborhood from a plague is 'small' compared to it. Instead, this man's quiet חסד in helping people bury their dead earned the protection. The reward fits the deed: he helped with death, so death was kept away.

keyTerms.meaning: It was shown to them, it was revealed to them
A hoe and a shovel (digging tools)

steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that simple, everyday חסד can protect a whole community, just like the merit of a great צדיק.

phrases.english: It was shown to them in a dream:
Rav, whose merit is very great —
this matter is too small for Rav.
Rather, it was because of a certain man
who lends a hoe and shovel for burial.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the assumption made in step 10.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The idea that רב's merit saved the neighborhood.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רב's merit is too great for such a small matter. The true cause was a simple man's kindness.

steps.title: Fire in דרוקרת spares רב הונא's neighborhood
steps.stepSummary: A fire broke out in דרוקרת, but it did not reach רב הונא's neighborhood. People assumed this was because of רב הונא's great merit.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a fire in דרוקרת, but in רב הונא's neighborhood there was no fire. People concluded that this was in the merit of רב הונא, which is great.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story that follows the same pattern as the first. This step sets up the assumption, and the next step will correct it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story matches the סורא story exactly. Only the disaster (a fire instead of a plague) and the רב (רב הונא instead of רב) are different. It is the same town of דרוקרת from earlier in the sugya.

phrases.english: In Drokart there was a fire,

phrases.aramaic: וּבְשִׁיבָבוּתֵיהּ דְּרַב הוּנָא לָא הֲווֹת דְּלֵיקְתָּא.
phrases.english: but in Rav Huna's neighborhood there was no fire.
They assumed from this
that it was in the merit of Rav Huna, which is great.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel second story built on the same pattern as steps 10–11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: People assumed רב הונא's neighborhood was spared in his merit.

steps.title: The dream: it was the woman who shared her oven
steps.stepSummary: A dream revealed that this was too small a matter for רב הונא's merit. The real cause was a woman who heated her oven and let her neighbors use it.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was shown to them in a dream: This is too small a thing for רב הונא. Rather, it was because of a certain woman who heats her oven and lets her neighbors use it.
steps.whatsHappening: A dream again corrects what people assumed. The neighborhood was saved by a simple woman's kindness, not by רב הונא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like the first story, the great רב's merit is 'too big' for this kind of rescue. The woman shared her fire, her heated oven, with others, so she was rewarded by being spared from fire. Again the reward matches the deed.
steps.whatToRemember: In both stories, a disaster passes over a neighborhood. Everyone credits the famous רב, but Heaven reveals that the protection came from an ordinary person's חסד. Each reward matched the deed: burial tools for a plague, and a shared oven for a fire.
steps.whyThisMatters: These stories close the section with a moral lesson. Small acts of kindness have great power, and we should never assume we know whose merit protects a community.

phrases.english: It was shown to them in a dream:
this is too small for Rav Huna;
rather, it was because of a certain woman
who heats her oven and lends it to her neighbors.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the assumption made in step 12, just as step 11 rejected step 10.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The idea that רב הונא's merit saved the neighborhood from the fire.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רב הונא's merit is too great for such a small matter. The true cause was a woman's generosity with her oven.

steps.title: רב יהודה decrees a fast because locusts arrived
steps.stepSummary: People tell רב יהודה that locusts have come, and he decrees a fast.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to רב יהודה: 'Locusts have come.' He decreed a fast.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new set of stories. רב יהודה hears that locusts have arrived and immediately declares a תענית. This sets up the challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Locusts are one of the classic disasters that call for a public fast. The story begins simply so that the next line can question whether a fast was really needed yet.

phrases.english: They said to Rav Yehuda:
Locusts have come.
He decreed a fast.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from stories of hidden merit protecting a neighborhood to stories about when sages decreed fasts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Locusts arriving is enough to decree a fast.

steps.title: The people object that the locusts are not causing damage
steps.stepSummary: The people protest that the locusts are not destroying anything, so a fast seems unnecessary.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: 'They are not causing any damage.'
steps.whatsHappening: The people push back on רב יהודה. They say the locusts are only eating a little and are not really harming the crops.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The objection is that a fast is for real damage, and nothing has been destroyed yet. If there is no harm, why fast?

keyTerms.meaning: they are not causing loss / destroying

phrases.english: They said to him: They are not causing damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the fast decreed in step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's decision to fast over locusts
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: No damage has happened yet, so there is no disaster to fast about.

steps.title: Did they bring their own food with them?
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה answers that the locusts did not bring provisions, so they will soon eat the crops.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: 'Did they bring food along with them?'
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers with a sharp question. The locusts did not pack lunch, so they will certainly end up eating your fields.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The danger is not measured by what has been eaten so far but by what is sure to come. Locusts that arrive will eat, so the threat is already real.

phrases.english: He said to them:
Did they bring provisions with them?
phrases.notes: A rhetorical question: obviously not, so they will eat your crops.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframing the danger as future and certain
steps.terutzHavaAmina: No damage yet means no reason to fast.
steps.terutzMaskana: Locusts will inevitably eat, so their arrival alone is a disaster worth fasting over.

steps.title: רב יהודה decrees a fast over a plague among pigs
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה hears of a plague among pigs and decrees a fast.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to רב יהודה: 'There is a plague among the pigs.' He decreed a fast.
steps.whatsHappening: A second story about רב יהודה. Animals are dying, not people, yet he decrees a תענית. This sets up the גמרא's question about why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A plague affecting only animals seems far removed from human danger. The surprise here is that the fast is over pigs, and the גמרא will try to understand his reasoning.

phrases.english: They said to Rav Yehuda:
There is a plague among the pigs.
He decreed a fast.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ לְרַב יְהוּדָה: אִיכָּא מוֹתָנָא בַּחֲזִירֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story, also about רב יהודה decreeing a fast.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A plague among pigs prompted a fast.

steps.title: Does רב יהודה hold that a plague in one species spreads to all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that רב יהודה believes a plague striking one species will spread to every species.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say that רב יהודה holds that a plague sent against one species is sent against all species?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to explain רב יהודה's fast with a general rule: a plague in any one kind of animal will spread to all kinds, including people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If this were his view, then any animal plague would be a reason to fast. The phrase נימא signals a suggestion that the גמרא will likely reject.

keyTerms.meaning: shall we say (introduces a suggestion that is usually rejected)
he holds, he is of the opinion
a plague that has been sent (a spreading affliction)

steps.confusionAlert: נימא does not tell you רב יהודה's real view. It is a trial suggestion, and the next line rejects it.

phrases.english: Shall we say that Rav Yehuda holds
that a plague sent against one species
is sent against all species?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to derive a general principle from the story in step 17.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רב יהודה's fast shows he holds that a plague in one species spreads to all species.

steps.title: No, pigs are different because their insides resemble humans
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the general rule. Pigs are a special case because their intestines are like a person's, so their disease can reach people.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Pigs are different, because their intestines are similar to those of human beings.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says we cannot learn a general rule from this story. רב יהודה fasted only because pigs are special.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Pigs' internal organs resemble human organs, so a disease killing pigs may also strike people. For other animals there may be no concern, so רב יהודה does not need to hold the broad rule.

phrases.english: No, pigs are different —
for their intestines are similar to those of human beings.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference proposed in step 18.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects learning a general 'one species, all species' rule from the pig story.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The pig case is unique, since pigs are physically similar to humans, so it cannot prove a rule about all animal plagues.
steps.whyThisMatters: Shows a classic move: a story or ruling based on a special feature cannot be stretched into a broad general principle.

steps.title: שמואל decrees a fast over a plague in בי חוזאי
steps.stepSummary: שמואל hears of a plague in בי חוזאי, a distant region, and decrees a fast.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to שמואל: 'There is a plague in בי חוזאי.' He decreed a fast.
steps.whatsHappening: A new story, now with שמואל. The plague is in a faraway place, yet he decrees a fast at home. This sets up the objection that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בי חוזאי was a region quite far from שמואל's community in בבל. The story tests whether distance makes a plague irrelevant.

keyTerms.meaning: בי חוזאי, a region far from the centers of בבל

phrases.english: They said to Shmuel:
There is a plague in Bei Chozai.
He decreed a fast.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ לִשְׁמוּאֵל: אִיכָּא מוֹתָנָא בֵּי חוֹזָאֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story about a different sage decreeing a fast.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שמואל decreed a fast over a plague in a distant region.

steps.title: But it is far away!
steps.stepSummary: People object that בי חוזאי is far, so the plague should not concern them.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: 'But it is far away!'
steps.whatsHappening: The people challenge שמואל. The plague is far from here, so why fast?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The objection assumes that distance alone protects a place from a plague. If so, there would be no local danger and no reason to fast.

phrases.english: They said to him: But it is far away!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the fast decreed in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's fast over a distant plague
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A faraway plague is no threat to us, so a fast seems pointless.

steps.title: There is no river crossing to stop it
steps.stepSummary: שמואל answers that there is no crossing or barrier between there and here to stop the plague.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: 'There is no crossing here that will cut it off.'
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל explains that distance alone is not protection. Nothing in between, such as a river crossing, blocks the plague from spreading to them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: What matters is not how far away a plague is, but whether something separates the places. With no barrier, the plague can travel all the way, so the danger is real.

keyTerms.meaning: a crossing, a river ford (a natural barrier)

phrases.english: He said: There is no crossing here
that will cut it off.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר: לֵיכָּא מַעְבָּרָא הָכָא דְּפָסֵיק לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the relevant factor from distance to the presence of a barrier
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A distant plague cannot reach us.
steps.terutzMaskana: Without a separating barrier, even a distant plague is a real threat.

steps.title: רב נחמן decrees a fast over a plague in ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן hears of a plague in ארץ ישראל and decrees a fast in בבל.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to רב נחמן: 'There is a plague in ארץ ישראל.' He decreed a fast.
steps.whatsHappening: The last story. The plague is in ארץ ישראל, very far from בבל, yet רב נחמן decrees a fast. His reason comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ארץ ישראל is very far from בבל, yet רב נחמן still decrees a fast. He will give a reason based on the status of the two lands, not on physical distance.

phrases.english: They said to Rav Nachman:
There is a plague in the Land of Israel.
He decreed a fast

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ לְרַב נַחְמָן: אִיכָּא מוֹתָנָא בְּאַרְעָא דְיִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story continuing the theme of fasting over distant plagues.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A plague in ארץ ישראל was reason enough to fast in בבל.

steps.title: If the lady is struck, surely the maidservant will be
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן explains with a קל וחומר: if ארץ ישראל (the lady) suffers, בבל (the maidservant) will surely suffer too.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: 'If the lady of the house is struck, all the more so the maidservant!'
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן gives the reason for his fast. ארץ ישראל is like the mistress of the house and בבל is like her servant, so a plague there surely threatens here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a קל וחומר. ארץ ישראל is holier and more protected, so if even it is struck, the less protected בבל is in greater danger. Unlike שמואל's reasoning about physical barriers, this argument is based on spiritual status.

keyTerms.meaning: the lady/mistress of the house (here, ארץ ישראל)

steps.whatToRemember: All four stories teach the same lesson: a threat that seems small, indirect, or distant can still call for a fast. This applies to locusts that have not yet eaten, a plague among pigs, a plague with no barrier between there and here, and a plague in ארץ ישראל, which surely endangers בבל.

phrases.english: He said: If the lady is struck,
is the maidservant not all the more so!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר: אִם גְּבִירָה לוֹקָה, שִׁפְחָה לֹא כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides רב נחמן's reasoning for the fast in step 23.
steps.raayaObject: Justifying a fast in בבל over a plague in ארץ ישראל
steps.raayaSupportSource: A קל וחומר based on ארץ ישראל being the 'lady' and בבל the 'maidservant'

steps.title: Does רב נחמן's reasoning clash with שמואל's fast?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא infers that רב נחמן's קל וחומר only applies to a 'lady and maidservant' case. Two places of equal standing should not need a fast for each other. But שמואל fasted for a plague in בי חוזאי, which was not a 'lady' to his city.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason is only because it was a lady (ארץ ישראל) and a maidservant (בבל). This implies that for a maidservant and a maidservant, two places in בבל, we would not fast. But they told שמואל there was a plague in בי חוזאי, and he decreed a fast!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws an inference from רב נחמן's reasoning. It then shows that this inference contradicts the earlier story about שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן fasted only because ארץ ישראל is greater than בבל, so if it suffers, בבל surely will. That implies two equal places, like two towns in בבל, do not affect each other. Yet שמואל fasted for בי חוזאי, which is an equal 'maidservant' to his city, so the inference seems wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: Maidservant (here, the lands outside ארץ ישראל)

phrases.english: The reason is because it is a lady and a maidservant,
which implies that for a maidservant and a maidservant — no.
phrases.notes: An inference from רב נחמן's reasoning.

phrases.english: But they said to שמואל:
There is a plague in בי חוזאי,
and he decreed a fast!
phrases.notes: בי חוזאי was not greater than שמואל's city, yet he fasted.

steps.triggerLanguage: טַעְמָא דִּגְבִירָה וְשִׁפְחָה, הָא שִׁפְחָה וְשִׁפְחָה — לָא. וְהָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from רב נחמן's קל וחומר in step 24 and sets it against שמואל's fast in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The implied limit of רב נחמן's reasoning: that only a 'lady' place suffering affects a 'maidservant' place.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שמואל fasted for an equal-status place, בי חוזאי. This shows that a plague in one 'maidservant' place does concern another.

steps.title: Caravans could carry the plague
steps.stepSummary: שמואל's case is different. Caravans regularly traveled from בי חוזאי, and the plague could come along with them.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there. Since there are caravans that travel together, the plague comes along with them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction. It explains that שמואל fasted for a practical reason, not because of status.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two equal places normally do not affect each other. But בי חוזאי had regular caravan traffic to שמואל's city, so the plague could physically travel along. This also explains what שמואל meant in step 22 when he said there was no barrier between there and here.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different there (a standard answer formula)

steps.whatToRemember: There are two reasons to fast for a plague somewhere else. One is status: if the 'lady' (ארץ ישראל) suffers, the 'maidservant' (בבל) surely will. The other is a real physical link, like caravans, between the two places.

phrases.english: It is different there,
since there are caravans
that travel along, and it (the plague) comes with them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case (שאני התם): a special factual feature, caravan traffic, explains שמואל's fast
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שמואל's fast proves that any two equal places affect each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: שמואל fasted only because caravans created a real physical route for the plague.

steps.title: אבא אומנא received greetings from Heaven every day
steps.stepSummary: A new story begins. אבא אומנא, a bloodletter, received greetings from the Heavenly yeshiva every day. אביי received them only every Friday, and רבא only every ערב יום כיפור.
steps.simpleTranslation: אבא אומנא (the bloodletter) would receive a greeting from the ישיבה of Heaven every day. אביי received one every Friday, and רבא every ערב יום כיפור.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story about a simple person whose good deeds earned special honor from Heaven. This sets up the question of why he deserved it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The surprise is that a bloodletter received more frequent Heavenly honor than great scholars like אביי and רבא. This continues the theme of the earlier stories, which show the great merit of ordinary people.

keyTerms.meaning: The yeshiva on High (the Heavenly academy)

phrases.aramaic: אַבָּא אוּמָּנָא הֲוָה אָתֵי לֵיהּ שְׁלָמָא
phrases.english: To Abba the bloodletter there would come a greeting
from the Heavenly yeshiva every day,
and to Abaye every Shabbat eve,
and to Rava every Yom Kippur eve.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַבָּא אוּמָּנָא הֲוָה אָתֵי לֵיהּ שְׁלָמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new אגדה about the merit of ordinary people.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אבא אומנא received Heavenly greetings more often than the great אמוראים אביי and רבא.

steps.title: אביי is told he cannot match אבא אומנא's deeds
steps.stepSummary: אביי was upset that אבא אומנא was honored more than he was. Heaven told him that he could not do what אבא אומנא does.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי was distressed because of אבא אומנא. They said to him: You are not able to do what he does.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי is bothered by the difference in honor, and Heaven answers him. This sets up the גמרא's next question: what exactly were these deeds?
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי's distress acts as an unspoken question: why does a bloodletter get more honor than a great scholar? The answer is that אבא אומנא's particular deeds were beyond what אביי could do. It does not say אבא אומנא was a greater scholar.

phrases.english: Abaye was distressed
because of Abba the bloodletter.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: לָא מָצֵית לְמִיעְבַּד כְּעוֹבָדֵיהּ.
phrases.english: They said to him: You are not able to do as his deeds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the unequal honor described in step 27.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: אבא אומנא's honor came from deeds that אביי could not match.

steps.title: What were אבא אומנא's deeds?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what these special deeds of אבא אומנא were.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what were the deeds of אבא אומנא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question. It is setting up a list of his righteous practices.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Heaven's answer to אביי was general. The גמרא now wants the details, which follow in the next steps.

phrases.english: And what were the deeds of Abba the bloodletter?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for details of the deeds mentioned in step 28.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The specific deeds that earned אבא אומנא his daily Heavenly greeting.

steps.title: His care for modesty during bloodletting
steps.stepSummary: אבא אומנא treated men and women separately. He also had a special garment with a slit at the incision point, so women patients would not be exposed.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he did bloodletting, he kept men separate from women. He had a garment with a slit where the incision was made. When a woman came to him, he had her wear it so that he would not look at her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the first answer: his strong care for צניעות (modesty) while working.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bloodletting required exposing skin. אבא אומנא went out of his way to protect his patients' modesty. He separated men and women and made a special garment so he would not see a woman exposed.

phrases.english: That when he would do the matter (bloodletting),

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה מַחֵית גַּבְרֵי לְחוֹד וְנָשֵׁי לְחוֹד,
phrases.english: he would bring in men separately and women separately,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִית לֵיהּ לְבוּשָׁא דְּאִית בֵּיהּ קַרְנָא
phrases.english: and he had a garment that had a horn (bloodletting point) in it
which was slit at the place of the incision.
When a woman would come to him,
he would dress her in it
so that he would not look at her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the question in step 29.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He guarded modesty by separating men and women and using a special slit garment.

steps.title: A hidden box so the poor would not be embarrassed
steps.stepSummary: Patients put their payment in a hidden place. Those who had money paid, and those who did not were never embarrassed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He had a hidden place where people would put the coins he charged. Whoever had money put it in, and whoever did not was not embarrassed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second deed: his care for the dignity of poor patients.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nobody could see who paid and who did not. This let poor people get treatment without shame, even though it meant אבא אומנא would lose money.

phrases.english: And he had a hidden place
where the coins that he took were thrown,
so one who had money would throw it in,
and one who did not have was not embarrassed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second deed to the answer begun in step 30.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He protected the poor from shame with a hidden payment place.

steps.title: Free treatment and money for Torah scholars
steps.stepSummary: אבא אומנא did not charge a תלמיד חכם. After the treatment, he even gave the scholar money to buy food and recover.
steps.simpleTranslation: When a young Torah scholar came to him, he took no payment. After the scholar got up, he gave him coins and said: Go and strengthen yourself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third deed: his special generosity toward Torah scholars.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He did more than waive his fee. He actually paid the scholar so he could buy healthy food, which a person needs after bloodletting. This shows his honor for Torah learners.

keyTerms.meaning: Go and heal or strengthen yourself

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֲוָה אִתְרְמֵי לֵיהּ צוּרְבָּא מֵרַבָּנַן,
phrases.english: When a young Torah scholar happened to come to him,
he would not take payment from him.
And after he got up, he would give him coins
and say to him: Go, strengthen yourself (with food).

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הֲוָה אִתְרְמֵי לֵיהּ צוּרְבָּא מֵרַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third deed to the list answering step 29.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He treated Torah scholars for free and gave them money to recover.

steps.title: אביי sends two scholars to test אבא אומנא
steps.stepSummary: אביי sent a pair of scholars to test אבא אומנא. He seated them, fed them, gave them drink, and laid out mats for them to sleep on at night.
steps.simpleTranslation: One day אביי sent a pair of רבנן to test him. He seated them, fed them, gave them drink, and spread out mats for them at night.
steps.whatsHappening: The story moves forward: אביי tests אבא אומנא, who first shows warm hospitality. This sets up the next part of the story, which continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי wanted to see for himself how righteous אבא אומנא really was. The scholars' visit is the setup for the test, and the hospitality here is only the first detail.

phrases.english: One day Abaye sent
a pair of Rabbis to test him.
He sat them down, fed them, and gave them drink,
and spread out mats for them at night.

steps.triggerLanguage: יוֹמָא חַד שַׁדַּר אַבָּיֵי זוּגָא דְרַבָּנַן לְמִיבְדְּקֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the אבא אומנא story with אביי's test of his righteousness.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אביי tests אבא אומנא, who welcomes the scholars with full hospitality.
